title: Food Webs and Ecosystems
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Food Webs and Ecosystems Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Use models of food webs to describe how energy flows through ecosystems and how organisms interact, and explain how human activities can affect these interactions (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on food webs and ecosystems: energy flow and pyramids, competition, predation, mutualism and parasitism, and introduced species such as cane toads and foxes. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Changes to one population spread through the whole food web.
body_html:
How to think about it

A food web shows how energy flows from producers to consumers in an ecosystem.

  • Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next; the rest is lost, mostly as heat.
  • Organisms interact through predation, competition, mutualism (both benefit) and parasitism (one is harmed).
  • Introduced species such as cane toads, rabbits, foxes and cats can upset Australian food webs.
Example

Producers have 10 000 kJ. About how much reaches herbivores?

about 10% passes on

Answer: about 1000 kJ

Example

A tick on a koala. Relationship?

the tick benefits

the koala is harmed

Answer: parasitism

Common mistakes

  • Thinking energy is recycled like matter.
  • Thinking removing predators always helps an ecosystem.
  • Calling every close relationship mutualism (in parasitism one is harmed).

faq.q: Why is energy lost along a food chain?
faq.a: Each organism uses most of the energy it takes in to live, move and keep warm. This energy is lost as heat, so only about 10% is passed on.

faq.q: Why are cane toads a problem?
faq.a: Cane toads are poisonous. Native predators such as quolls, goannas and some snakes die when they eat them, and the toads compete with native animals for food.

faq.q: What is the difference between mutualism and parasitism?
faq.a: In mutualism both organisms benefit. In parasitism the parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: Clownfish live among sea anemone tentacles and clean them; the anemone protects the clownfish. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both benefit.

items.q: What is an ecosystem?
c: only the animals in an area
all the living things in an area and their non-living surroundings
items.e: Living and non-living parts.

items.q: What do decomposers do?
c: break down dead organisms and waste, returning minerals to the soil
items.e: Bacteria and fungi.

items.q: Why does a food web with many species usually cope better with change?
c: If one food source is lost, animals can eat others.
items.e: Diversity makes ecosystems more stable.

items.q: Look at the food web of a billabong. In this web, the platypus eats yabbies and dragonfly nymphs. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Which human activity helps protect food webs?
c: removing feral animals and protecting habitats
items.e: Conservation keeps ecosystems balanced.

items.q: Is energy recycled in an ecosystem like matter is?
c: No. Energy flows through and is lost as heat; matter is recycled.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. In this web, the powerful owl eats possums. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: What is a food web?
items.e: More realistic.

items.q: Producers in a food chain trap 100 000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes to each next level. How much reaches the secondary consumers?
Crown-of-thorns starfish eat coral. What happens to a reef when their numbers explode?
c: Large areas of coral die, affecting the fish that depend on it.
items.e: One population change spreads through the food web.

Which organism is the producer?
items.e: It makes its own food by photosynthesis.

items.q: A tick feeds on a koala's blood. Which relationship is this?
items.e: The tick benefits; the koala is harmed.

items.q: Primary consumers take in 2000 kJ from producers but pass only 200 kJ to secondary consumers. Where does most of the rest go?
c: It is used in respiration for life processes and lost as heat.
It is recycled back to the producers.
It is stored in the Sun.
items.e: Energy flows through a food chain and is not recycled.

items.q: Producers in a food chain trap 50 000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes to each next level. How much reaches the secondary consumers?
What is a producer?
c: a plant or alga that makes its own food by photosynthesis
items.e: Start of every chain.

items.q: Producers in a food chain trap 20 000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes to each next level. How much reaches the secondary consumers?
Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the coral trout eats small fish. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. In this web, the possum eats gum trees. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: In a food chain, what do the arrows show?
c: what eats what, pointing at the food
the direction energy flows: from what is eaten to what eats it
items.e: Arrow means 'is eaten by'.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. A disease kills most of the kangaroos. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The dingo eats only a kangaroo in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a billabong. Most of the dragonfly nymphs are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the dragonfly nymph eats mosquito larvae in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. A disease kills most of the possums. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The powerful owl eats only a possum in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. A disease kills most of the native grass. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The ant eats only native grass in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. How many food chains are there in this food web?
items.e: Trace every path from a producer to an animal that nothing eats.

items.q: Look at the food web of a billabong. A disease kills most of the yabbies. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The Murray cod eats only a yabby in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Matilda reads: “A disease kills many of the bees in an orchard.” Predict what happens to the apple crop.
c: It will grow without any limit.
It will decrease because fewer flowers are pollinated.
It will turn into a different species.
It will stay exactly the same.
items.e: Changes in one population affect others it interacts with.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the small fish are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the small fish eats zooplankton in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the reef sharks are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the reef shark eats coral trout in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. Most of the kookaburras are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the kookaburra eats grasshoppers in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. Most of the powerful owls are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the powerful owl eats possums in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the coral trout are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the coral trout eats small fish in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. A disease kills most of the small fish. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The coral trout eats only a small fish in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. A disease kills most of the ants. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The thorny devil eats only an ant in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. How many kinds of food does the green turtle eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the green turtle.

items.q: Look at the food web of a billabong. A disease kills most of the waterweed. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The yabby eats only waterweed in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. Most of the bearded dragons are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the bearded dragon eats grasshoppers in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. How many food chains are there in this food web?
items.e: Trace every path from a producer to an animal that nothing eats.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. Most of the thorny devils are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the thorny devil eats ants in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Kai reads: “Many cats are released near a bird colony.” Predict what happens to the birds.
c: It will stay exactly the same.
It will grow without any limit.
It will turn into a different species.
It will decrease because of more predation.
items.e: Changes in one population affect others it interacts with.

items.q: What is competition?
c: a parasite living on a host
organisms trying to get the same limited resource
items.e: For example, kangaroos and rabbits compete for grass.

items.q: What is parasitism?
c: one organism hunts the other for food
a relationship in which the parasite benefits and the host is harmed
items.e: A tapeworm is a parasite.

items.q: Bees collect nectar from flowers and pollinate them. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both organisms benefit.

items.q: Head lice live on the human scalp and feed on blood. Which relationship is this?
items.e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: Oliver needs an example of predation (one organism hunts and eats another). Which is the best example?
c: cattle egrets eat insects stirred up by grazing cows
clownfish live in sea anemones and help keep them clean
a hawk dives for a rabbit
fungi on plant roots get sugar and help roots take in water
items.e: That is predation.

items.q: Amelia observes that cattle egrets eat insects stirred up by grazing cows. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: A python catches and eats rats. Which relationship is this?
items.e: One organism hunts and eats the other.

items.q: Which process traps the Sun's energy and brings it into an ecosystem?
items.e: Producers convert light energy into chemical energy.

items.q: A student uses a data logger with a light sensor in a forest and in an open field. What is she investigating?
c: how light intensity differs between the two habitats
the speed of the wind only
items.e: Probes can also measure temperature and pH.

items.q: Ethan needs an example of predation (one organism hunts and eats another). Which is the best example?
c: moss grows on the bark of a tree
a hermit crab lives in an empty snail shell
bacteria in your intestines get food and help you digest
items.e: That is predation.

items.q: Bacteria in a cow's gut digest cellulose; the bacteria get food and shelter. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both organisms benefit.

items.q: A shark hunts squid. Which relationship is this?
items.e: One organism hunts and eats the other.

items.q: Mosquitoes feed on human blood. Which relationship is this?
items.e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: A ladybird eats aphids on a hibiscus plant. Which relationship is this?
items.e: One organism hunts and eats the other.

items.q: Amelia observes that a ladybird eats aphids. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In predation, one organism hunts and eats another.

items.q: Amelia observes that a mosquito feeds on a person's blood. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Kai needs an example of mutualism (both benefit). Which is the best example?
c: a mosquito feeds on a person's blood
clownfish live in sea anemones and help keep them clean
cattle egrets eat insects stirred up by grazing cows
items.e: That is mutualism.

items.q: Priya needs an example of mutualism (both benefit). Which is the best example?
c: ants protect acacia trees and live in their thorns
trees grow taller to reach the same sunlight
a hawk dives for a rabbit
items.e: That is mutualism.

items.q: What is mutualism?
c: one organism benefits and the other is harmed
a relationship in which both organisms benefit
items.e: For example, bees and flowers.

items.q: Lachlan observes that mistletoe takes water and nutrients from a tree. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Seedlings grow towards a window. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Fish gather near the surface of a pond with very little dissolved oxygen. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Mangrove trees grow in salty, waterlogged mud with little oxygen. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Few plants grow on the dark floor of a dense rainforest. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Where does almost all the energy in an ecosystem come from?
items.e: Producers capture light energy.

items.q: Cacti survive in deserts where it rarely rains. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Why do food chains rarely have more than five links?
c: Animals run out of food at night.
Energy is made at each step.
Energy is lost at each step, mostly as heat, so little reaches the top.
items.e: Only about 10% passes on.

items.q: How do feral pigs harm Australian ecosystems?
c: They dig up soil and eat native plants and frogs.
They eat grasses and seedlings and compete with native herbivores, causing erosion.
They stir up mud in rivers, making the water cloudy for native fish.
They hunt small native mammals and ground-nesting birds.
items.e: Introduced species often have no natural predators here, so their numbers grow quickly.

items.e: The top predator: poison builds up at each level.

items.q: Which action helps pollinators?
c: planting wildflowers and leaving areas uncut
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

The food chain is algae → water flea → minnow → pike. Which organism has the lowest concentration?
items.e: The producer at the bottom.

items.q: How do European rabbits harm Australian ecosystems?
c: They dig up soil and eat native plants and frogs.
They hunt native birds, reptiles and small mammals.
They eat grasses and seedlings and compete with native herbivores, causing erosion.
They eat native insects and poison native predators such as quolls and goannas that eat them.
items.e: Introduced species often have no natural predators here, so their numbers grow quickly.

items.q: How do pesticides sprayed on crops sometimes harm bees?
c: They can poison bees that visit the flowers.
They have no effect on insects.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: What is interdependence?
c: Living things in an ecosystem depend on each other for food, shelter and pollination.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: Pitcher plants catch insects because the soil is poor in nitrogen. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

The food chain is algae → water flea → minnow → pike. How many times greater is the concentration in the minnow than in the water flea?
Why are insect pollinators such as bees important to farmers?
c: Many crops need insects to carry pollen so that fruits and seeds form.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: How do cane toads harm Australian ecosystems?
c: They hunt small native mammals and ground-nesting birds.
They eat native insects and poison native predators such as quolls and goannas that eat them.
They dig up soil and eat native plants and frogs.
They eat grasses and seedlings and compete with native herbivores, causing erosion.
items.e: Introduced species often have no natural predators here, so their numbers grow quickly.

items.q: How do red foxes harm Australian ecosystems?
c: They hunt native birds, reptiles and small mammals.
They hunt small native mammals and ground-nesting birds.
They eat grasses and seedlings and compete with native herbivores, causing erosion.
They stir up mud in rivers, making the water cloudy for native fish.
items.e: Introduced species often have no natural predators here, so their numbers grow quickly.

items.q: What could happen to apple harvests if bee numbers fall a lot?
c: Fewer flowers are pollinated, so fewer apples grow.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: A survey counts 1000 grasshoppers, 80 lizards and 5 kookaburras in a paddock. What does this pattern show?
c: Top predators are the most common.
There are fewer organisms at each higher feeding level.
items.e: Less energy reaches higher levels.

items.q: Rats were reduced on an island. Then the number of birds that nest on the ground rose. Why?
c: Fewer rats ate the birds' eggs and chicks.
items.e: Removing a predator affects its prey.

items.q: Mosquito fish are added to ponds to control mosquitoes. Which relationship is used?
items.e: The fish eat mosquito larvae.

items.q: Scientists count frogs in a wetland each spring for 10 years. Why collect data for so long?
c: to see real trends, not just changes from one year to the next
items.e: Long-term data shows patterns.

items.q: Foxes are removed from a reserve. Bilby numbers rise, then grass seeds become scarce. What is the best explanation?
c: More bilbies eat more seeds, so food becomes limited.
items.e: Changes pass along the web.

items.q: Corals turn white (bleach) when sea temperatures rise. What does this show?
c: A change in a physical factor can affect the survival of organisms.
Corals are plants that need more light.
items.e: Coral bleaching is linked to global warming.

items.q: Which method is best for estimating the number of plants in a large paddock?
c: count plants in several random 1 m squares (quadrats) and scale up
items.e: Sampling saves time and is reliable if random.

items.q: What is symbiosis?
c: a close, long-term relationship between two different species
items.e: Mutualism, commensalism and parasitism are types of symbiosis.

items.q: A farmer sprays a pesticide that kills all the insects in a field. Which is a likely result?
c: Birds that eat insects lose their food, and plants that need pollinators make fewer seeds.
items.e: Organisms in an ecosystem are interdependent.

items.q: If the number of predators increases, what usually happens to the prey?
items.e: More predators eat more prey.

items.q: Mia finds that cowbirds lay eggs in other birds' nests, and the other birds raise the cowbird chicks. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: The host birds are harmed.

items.q: What do organisms compete for?
c: limited resources like food, water, space, light and mates
items.e: Competition happens when resources are limited.

items.q: How do feral cats harm Australian ecosystems?
c: They eat grasses and seedlings and compete with native herbivores, causing erosion.
They eat native insects and poison native predators such as quolls and goannas that eat them.
They hunt small native mammals and ground-nesting birds.
They hunt native birds, reptiles and small mammals.
items.e: Introduced species often have no natural predators here, so their numbers grow quickly.

items.q: Why do similar interactions happen in very different ecosystems?
c: Organisms everywhere need food, shelter and mates, so they compete, hunt and cooperate.
items.e: Patterns repeat across ecosystems.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. A disease kills most of the zooplankton. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The small fish eats only zooplankton in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: A student says, 'Removing all predators is good for an ecosystem.' Why is this not correct?
c: Prey numbers can grow too large and eat out their food supply.
items.e: Predators help keep balance.

items.q: Why do some cultures leave fields to rest for a season or use crop rotation?
c: to make the soil more acidic
to let the soil recover its minerals, which is a sustainable practice
items.e: Sustainable practices protect ecosystems.

items.q: How do carp harm Australian ecosystems?
c: They eat grasses and seedlings and compete with native herbivores, causing erosion.
They hunt native birds, reptiles and small mammals.
They stir up mud in rivers, making the water cloudy for native fish.
They hunt small native mammals and ground-nesting birds.
items.e: Introduced species often have no natural predators here, so their numbers grow quickly.

items.q: Two species of barnacles live on the same rock. When one is removed, the other spreads into its area. What does this show?
items.e: Removing a competitor frees resources.

items.q: Why do scientists study interactions before bringing a new species into an area?
c: The new species may compete with, eat or harm native species.
items.e: Predicting interactions prevents problems.
